Appendix A Extended Related Work and Positioning

This appendix expands Section 5 with a technical positioning of hh-control against the four research lines it sits between: camera-controllable video generation, training-free conditional sampling on pretrained diffusion/flow models, plug-and-play denoiser-as-prior methods, and generalized denoising auto-encoders.

A.1 Camera-controllable video generation

Training-based controllers.

CameraCtrl [He et al., 2024] and CameraCtrl II [He et al., 2025] inject Plücker-coordinate camera embeddings into a CogVideoX-style backbone. VD3D [Bahmani et al., 2024] and AC3D [Bahmani et al., 2025] train video DiTs with explicit 3D-aware tokenization. MotionCtrl [Wang et al., 2024] trains a separate motion module conditioned on camera and object motion fields. Multi-view extensions: SyncCammaster [Bai et al., 2024] synchronizes generation across views, and ReCamMaster [Bai et al., 2025] learns to re-render an input video under a new trajectory by joint training on synchronized multi-camera data. Several systems build a 4D scaffold from a source video and guide the generator with it: TrajectoryAttention [Xiao et al., 2024] introduces trajectory-aware attention; TrajectoryCrafter [Yu et al., 2025] renders explicit point clouds from monocular input and trains a refinement diffusion model on top. ViewCrafter [Yu et al., 2024] and Vid-camedit [Seo et al., 2025] solve sparse-view novel-view synthesis by combining explicit 3D priors with generative refinement; Van Hoorick et al. [2024] provides a generative-modeling perspective on the same problem. The common requirement across this family is that at least one component — backbone, adapter, or refinement head — is fine-tuned to internalize the trajectory-to-video correspondence.

Training-free controllers.

TTM [Singer et al., 2025] and WorldForge [Song et al., 2025] construct a warped guidance video by lifting the source to a point cloud through monocular depth and reprojecting under the target camera, then run a pretrained generator with hard latent replacement on the visibility mask at every denoising step. Recapture [Zhang et al., 2025] and Latent Reframing [Zhou et al., 2025] use a similar warp-and-replace primitive with mask construction tuned for static scenes. Zero4D [Park et al., 2025] extends this to free-camera 4D generation in a zero-shot fashion, again via masked replacement. Coarse-Guided [Wang et al., 2026] drops the partial mask and instead applies a global noise-aware soft pull toward the warped reference. Both ends of this spectrum are degenerate boundary limits of hh-control: at σy→0\sigma_{y}\!\to\!0 the warp likelihood concentrates on {z0:M⊙z0=M⊙z~0}\{z_{0}:M\!\odot\!z_{0}=M\!\odot\!\tilde{z}_{0}\} and the write-back collapses to hard replacement; at M≡1M\!\equiv\!1 the partial mask becomes the whole grid and the soft pull reduces to Coarse-Guided. These are sanity-check consistency properties, not the regime where hh-control operates. The novel object is the interior: at finite σy\sigma_{y} on a non-trivial partial mask, the inner block-conditional Gibbs refinement targets the partial-observation conditional posterior p⁡(z0|1−M​∣z¯t|M)p(z_{0}|_{1-M}\!\mid\!\bar{z}_{t}|_{M}) (Proposition 1), which has no counterpart in either baseline and is what delivers the gains in Section 4.1.

A.2 Training-free conditional sampling

First-order surrogates: DPS family.

Diffusion Posterior Sampling [Chung et al., 2022] replaces the intractable hh-induced drift with the gradient of the observation likelihood evaluated at the Tweedie mean z^0\hat{z}_{0}. A line of follow-ups substitutes alternative point estimates for z^0\hat{z}_{0} or alternative likelihoods (FreeDoM, Π\PiGDM, MPGD [He et al., 2023], TFG-UGD), all sharing the property that the surrogate is a single point evaluation of ∇log⁡h\nabla\log h. Position of hh-control: the outer step is exactly a DPS-style surrogate restricted to the partial mask MM; the structural addition is the inner block-conditional Gibbs refinement on −M1\!-\!M.

Noise-aware weighted surrogates.

The DPS surrogate is most reliable at high σt\sigma_{t} and degrades as σt→0\sigma_{t}\!\to\!0, where z^0\hat{z}_{0} becomes deterministic. Weighted hh-transform sampling [Wang et al., 2026] introduces a noise-level-aware scalar λσt\lambda_{\sigma_{t}} that down-weights the surrogate at low noise. DEFT [Denker et al., 2024] amortizes the surrogate by training a small network that predicts the hh-induced drift directly, and Zhu et al. [2026] fine-tunes the base model to internalize the same drift. Position of hh-control: we extend the global scalar λσt\lambda_{\sigma_{t}} to a spatially non-uniform mask MM and pair it with a novel inner refinement on the unobserved support, while keeping the conditioning entirely at inference time — no extra network and no fine-tuning.

Sequential Monte Carlo and Feynman–Kac.

Twisted Diffusion Samplers [Wu et al., 2023] and Feynman–Kac steering [Singhal et al., 2025] maintain a population of trajectories and reweight them by the running terminal compatibility, recovering an unbiased estimator of ∇log⁡ht\nabla\log h_{t} in the large-particle limit. The price is N×N\!\times inference compute per step. Position of hh-control: the inner Gibbs chain is a single-trajectory variance-reduction primitive operating on the same physical sample, achieving similar conditional adherence at a small per-step multiplier rather than N×N\!\times.

A.3 Plug-and-play and denoiser-as-prior methods

PnP-ADMM [Sreehari et al., 2016], RED [Romano et al., 2017], and score-based extensions [Hu et al., 2023, Terris et al., 2025] share the “denoiser as implicit prior” perspective: a pretrained denoiser is invoked at a single fixed noise level inside a half-quadratic or proximal solver, acting as a projection-onto-prior step against a hard data-fidelity constraint. hh-control reuses the same intuition but in a structurally different setting — a multi-step flow-matching sampler with a time-varying schedule, where the implicit prior is queried at every σt\sigma_{t} and conditioned on a partial observation, so the inner chain targets p⁡(z0|1−M​∣z¯t|M)p(z_{0}|_{1-M}\!\mid\!\bar{z}_{t}|_{M}) rather than the unconditional data law that PnP targets.

Appendix B Flow matching and Doob’s hh-transform background

This appendix expands the brief summary in Section 2 into a self-contained derivation, starting from score-based diffusion as a forward SDE, deriving the velocity–score identity that underwrites flow matching, and arriving at the controlled flow-matching velocity used in Eq. (5) of the method section. Readers fluent in score-based diffusion and Doob’s hh-transform can skip directly to Section B.4.

B.1 Score-based diffusion via SDEs

Score-based generative models [Song et al., 2021] cast sampling as the time reversal of a noising SDE that transports data z0∼p0z_{0}\!\sim\!p_{0} to a tractable prior pT=𝒩⁡(0,I)p_{T}\!=\!\mathcal{N}(0,I):

d​zt=f⁡(zt,t)​d​t+g⁡(t)​d​wt,t∈[0,T],dz_{t}\;=\;f(z_{t},t)\,dt\;+\;g(t)\,dw_{t},\qquad t\in[0,T], (14)

with drift ff, diffusion coefficient gg, and Wiener process wtw_{t}. Its time-reversed dynamics [Anderson, 1982], integrated from zT∼pTz_{T}\!\sim\!p_{T} back to t=0t\!=\!0, recover samples from p0p_{0}:

d​zt=[f⁡(zt,t)−g​(t)2​∇zt​log⁡pt​(zt)]​d​t+g⁡(t)​d​w¯t,dz_{t}\;=\;\bigl[f(z_{t},t)-g(t)^{2}\,\nabla_{z_{t}}\log p_{t}(z_{t})\bigr]\,dt\;+\;g(t)\,d\bar{w}_{t}, (15)

where ptp_{t} is the marginal of ztz_{t} and w¯t\bar{w}_{t} a reverse-time Wiener process. The score ∇zt​log​pt\nabla_{z_{t}}\log p_{t} is learned as sθ​(zt,t)s_{\theta}(z_{t},t) via denoising score matching [Vincent, 2011]. The same marginals {pt}\{p_{t}\} can be induced by the deterministic probability-flow ODE [Song et al., 2021],

d​zt=[f⁡(zt,t)−12​g​(t)2​∇zt​log⁡pt​(zt)]​d​t.dz_{t}\;=\;\bigl[f(z_{t},t)-\tfrac{1}{2}\,g(t)^{2}\,\nabla_{z_{t}}\log p_{t}(z_{t})\bigr]\,dt. (16)

B.2 Flow matching as reparameterization, and the velocity–score identity

Flow matching [Lipman et al., 2022, Liu et al., 2022] is equivalent to a reparameterization of the probability-flow ODE Eq. (16). Choosing the variance-exploding coefficients [Song et al., 2021] f⁡(zt,t)=(σ˙t/σt)​ztf(z_{t},t)\!=\!(\dot{\sigma}_{t}/\sigma_{t})\,z_{t} and g⁡(t)=2​σ˙t​σtg(t)\!=\!\sqrt{2\,\dot{\sigma}_{t}\,\sigma_{t}} in Eq. (14) produces marginals zt=(−σt)​z0+σt​ϵz_{t}\!=\!(1\!-\!\sigma_{t})z_{0}+\sigma_{t}\epsilon with ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\epsilon\!\sim\!\mathcal{N}(0,I) along a monotone schedule σ0=0,σ1=1\sigma_{0}\!=\!0,\sigma_{1}\!=\!1. Substituting these into Eq. (16) reduces it to the deterministic ODE d​zt/d​t=uθ​(zt,t,c)dz_{t}/dt\!=\!u_{\theta}(z_{t},t,c) through the velocity–score identity

uθ​(zt,t,c)=σ˙tσt​zt−σ˙t​σt​∇zt​log⁡pt​(zt∣c),u_{\theta}(z_{t},t,c)\;=\;\frac{\dot{\sigma}_{t}}{\sigma_{t}}\,z_{t}\;-\;\dot{\sigma}_{t}\,\sigma_{t}\,\nabla_{z_{t}}\log p_{t}(z_{t}\mid c), (17)

where cc is the external condition (e.g., text for T2V). Flow matching trains uθu_{\theta} to regress ϵ−z0\epsilon\!-\!z_{0}; sampling integrates the ODE backward from z1∼𝒩⁡(0,I)z_{1}\!\sim\!\mathcal{N}(0,I) to z0z_{0}. Eq. (17) is the load-bearing bridge in hh-control’s derivation: every step that adds an hh-induced drift to the score in Eq. (2) can be rewritten as an additive correction to uθu_{\theta}, giving the controlled velocity Eq. (3). The plug-in clean-prediction estimator Eq. (1) follows from Eq. (17) by Tweedie’s identity z^0​(zt)=zt+σt2​∇zt​log⁡pt​(zt)\hat{z}_{0}(z_{t})\!=\!z_{t}+\sigma_{t}^{2}\nabla_{z_{t}}\log p_{t}(z_{t}) and the forward parameterization above.

B.3 Doob’s hh-transform for conditional sampling

Many practical tasks impose an endpoint constraint on the reverse SDE rather than just a terminal distribution — for instance, the noisy inverse problem y=𝒜⁡(z0)+ny\!=\!\mathcal{A}(z_{0})+n with known operator 𝒜\mathcal{A}, observation yy, and noise nn. Conditioning the marginals ptp_{t} in Eq. (15) on such an event is intractable, since the conditional dynamics couples through all future steps. Doob’s hh-transform [Rogers and Williams, 2000] resolves this by tilting the unconditioned path measure with a non-negative terminal weight h⁡(z0)h(z_{0}) — e.g. the indicator 𝟏B​(z0)\mathbf{1}_{B}(z_{0}) for hard conditioning, or the likelihood p⁡(y∣z0)p(y\!\mid\!z_{0}) for soft conditioning on yy — yielding a Markov diffusion whose endpoint follows the desired conditional and whose drift carries an additive correction.

Following Denker et al. [2024], Wang et al. [2026], define the time-dependent hh-function as the conditional expectation of the terminal weight:

ht​(zt)=𝔼⁡[h⁡(z0)|zt]=∫p0|t​(z0∣zt)​h​(z0)​d​z0,h_{t}(z_{t})\;=\;\mathbb{E}\!\bigl[\,h(z_{0})\,\bigm|\,z_{t}\bigr]\;=\;\int p_{0|t}(z_{0}\!\mid\!z_{t})\,h(z_{0})\,dz_{0}, (18)

where p0|tp_{0|t} is the unconditional posterior of the clean endpoint given the current state. Doob’s theorem yields the conditioned reverse SDE Eq. (2) with an additive hh-induced drift ∇zt​log​ht​(zt)\nabla_{z_{t}}\log h_{t}(z_{t}), and via Eq. (17) the controlled flow-matching velocity Eq. (3). For the noisy inverse problem with h⁡(z0)=p⁡(y∣z0)h(z_{0})\!=\!p(y\!\mid\!z_{0}), Eq. (18) specializes to ht​(zt)=pt​(y∣zt)h_{t}(z_{t})\!=\!p_{t}(y\!\mid\!z_{t}), recovering the standard posterior-sampling identity ∇zt​log​pt​(zt∣y)=∇zt​log​pt​(zt)+∇zt​log​pt​(y∣zt)\nabla_{z_{t}}\log p_{t}(z_{t}\!\mid\!y)\!=\!\nabla_{z_{t}}\log p_{t}(z_{t})+\nabla_{z_{t}}\log p_{t}(y\!\mid\!z_{t}) [Denker et al., 2024].

B.4 Tractable surrogates for ∇log⁡ht\nabla\log h_{t}

The hh-induced drift ∇zt​log​ht​(zt)\nabla_{z_{t}}\log h_{t}(z_{t}) in Eq. (2) is intractable in general, since evaluating the hh-function Eq. (18) requires the unconditional posterior p0|tp_{0|t} of a large pretrained model and a marginalization over future trajectories. Practical conditional sampling therefore replaces ∇log⁡ht\nabla\log h_{t} with a tractable surrogate. The useful taxonomic axis turns out to be whether the surrogate backpropagates through the denoiser to compute its gradient; we group the established families along this axis and locate hh-control among them.

Common first-order point surrogate.

All single-trajectory families below share the same starting point: replace the intractable expectation in Eq. (18) by hh evaluated at the Tweedie posterior mean z^0​(zt)\hat{z}_{0}(z_{t}) (Eq. (1)),

ht​(zt)≈h⁡(z^0​(zt))⟹∇zt​log​ht​(zt)≈∇zt​log​h​(z^0​(zt)).h_{t}(z_{t})\;\approx\;h\bigl(\hat{z}_{0}(z_{t})\bigr)\;\Longrightarrow\;\nabla_{z_{t}}\log h_{t}(z_{t})\;\approx\;\nabla_{z_{t}}\log h\bigl(\hat{z}_{0}(z_{t})\bigr). (19)

The chain rule expands the right-hand side as

∇zt​log​h​(z^0​(zt))=(∇z^0​log​h)​(z^0​(zt))⏟cheap, no autograd⋅∇ztz^0​(zt)⏟=I−σt​∇ztuθ​(zt,t,c),\nabla_{z_{t}}\log h\bigl(\hat{z}_{0}(z_{t})\bigr)\;=\;\underbrace{\bigl(\nabla_{\hat{z}_{0}}\log h\bigr)\!\bigl(\hat{z}_{0}(z_{t})\bigr)}_{\text{cheap, no autograd}}\,\cdot\,\underbrace{\nabla_{z_{t}}\hat{z}_{0}(z_{t})}_{=\,I-\sigma_{t}\,\nabla_{z_{t}}u_{\theta}(z_{t},t,c)}, (20)

so a faithful evaluation requires the denoiser Jacobian ∇ztuθ\nabla_{z_{t}}u_{\theta}. Whether this Jacobian is computed in full or dropped is what distinguishes families (i) and (ii) below.

(i) Jacobian-aware first-order surrogates (gradient through the denoiser).

This family computes Eq. (20) in full, backpropagating through one or more denoiser forwards. Diffusion Posterior Sampling (DPS) [Chung et al., 2022] is the canonical instance: for a Gaussian observation h⁡(z0)=𝒩⁡(y,𝒜⁡(z0),τ2​I)h(z_{0})\!=\!\mathcal{N}(y;\mathcal{A}(z_{0}),\tau^{2}I) the surrogate becomes the gradient of a measurement-consistency loss with respect to ztz_{t}, computed by autograd through z^0​(zt)\hat{z}_{0}(z_{t}) and hence through uθu_{\theta}. Manifold Preserving Guided Diffusion (MPGD) [He et al., 2023] additionally projects the Jacobian-computed gradient onto the data-manifold tangent to prevent off-manifold drift. Training-Free Guidance with universal-guidance recurrence (TFG-UGD) [Ye et al., 2024] runs several inner mean-guidance iterations per outer step, each backpropagating through the denoiser. The defining feature of this family is the autograd-through-uθu_{\theta} requirement: each surrogate evaluation costs at least one denoiser-sized backward pass and the activations must be retained for backprop, so the memory footprint scales with the model and resolution. This is the price paid for using the full first-order Taylor expansion of log⁡h\log h around ztz_{t}.

(ii) Jacobian-free first-order surrogates (stop-grad through the denoiser).

This family uses the same point surrogate Eq. (19) but drops the Jacobian in Eq. (20): ∇ztz^0≈I\nabla_{z_{t}}\hat{z}_{0}\!\approx\!I, equivalent to detaching z^0\hat{z}_{0} from ztz_{t} before gradient computation. The surrogate then collapses to ∇zt​log​h​(z^0)≈∇z^0​log​h​(z^0)\nabla_{z_{t}}\log h(\hat{z}_{0})\!\approx\!\nabla_{\hat{z}_{0}}\log h(\hat{z}_{0}), which is cheap and requires no backprop through uθu_{\theta}. This “stop-grad” approximation is documented in DPS itself (see Chung et al. 2022, App. A) and is the standard choice for inference-time guidance on large pretrained backbones where the Jacobian-aware variant is computationally infeasible. Two strategies within this family compensate for the loss of Jacobian information. (a) Noise-aware weighting. Weighted hh-transform sampling [Wang et al., 2026] introduces λσt=σtα\lambda_{\sigma_{t}}\!=\!\sigma_{t}^{\alpha} on the surrogate,

∇zt​log​ht​(zt)≈λσt​∇z^0​log⁡h⁡(z^0​(zt)),\nabla_{z_{t}}\log h_{t}(z_{t})\;\approx\;\lambda_{\sigma_{t}}\,\nabla_{\hat{z}_{0}}\log h\bigl(\hat{z}_{0}(z_{t})\bigr), (21)

down-weighting at low σt\sigma_{t} where the Jacobian carries the most information and the stop-grad approximation degrades fastest. For coarse-guided flow-matching with h⁡(z0)∝δ⁡(z0−y~)h(z_{0})\!\propto\!\delta(z_{0}\!-\!\tilde{y}) replaced by a tractable proxy y~\tilde{y}, this yields the closed-form controlled velocity

utctrl=uθ+λσt​(zt−y~σt−uθ),u^{\text{ctrl}}_{t}\;=\;u_{\theta}\;+\;\lambda_{\sigma_{t}}\!\Bigl(\frac{z_{t}-\tilde{y}}{\sigma_{t}}-u_{\theta}\Bigr), (22)

interpolating between the pretrained velocity (λσt→0\lambda_{\sigma_{t}}\!\to\!0) and a hard pull toward the warped reference (λσt→1\lambda_{\sigma_{t}}\!\to\!1). (b) Amortized surrogate. DEFT [Denker et al., 2024] trains a small network to predict ∇zt​log​ht\nabla_{z_{t}}\log h_{t} directly, sidestepping the inference-time Jacobian by amortizing it offline; Zhu et al. [2026] fine-tunes the base model itself to internalize the same correction. Both incur an extra training stage but, like the weighted variant, avoid autograd through the pretrained denoiser at sampling time.

(iii) Particle-based surrogates (Sequential Monte Carlo / Feynman–Kac).

Twisted Diffusion Samplers [Wu et al., 2023] and Feynman–Kac steering [Singhal et al., 2025] maintain a population of trajectories and reweight them by the running terminal compatibility, recovering an unbiased estimate of ∇log⁡ht\nabla\log h_{t} in the large-particle limit at the cost of N×N\!\times inference compute per step. They are orthogonal to (i)/(ii) along the Jacobian axis: the bias of the surrogate is reduced by particle resampling rather than by a better single-point estimator, so neither the Jacobian nor a stop-grad proxy enters the picture.

B.5 Position of our work

hh-control belongs to family (ii) (Jacobian-free first-order surrogate): the surrogate is the Tweedie point estimate Eq. (19) with the denoiser Jacobian ∇ztuθ\nabla_{z_{t}}u_{\theta} dropped. The Jacobian-free choice is mandatory rather than optional in our setting — the Wan 2.2 backbone has ∼5\sim\!5B parameters at ××49720\!\times\!1280\!\times\!49 resolution, so each backward through uθu_{\theta} would dominate the per-step compute of any Jacobian-aware surrogate from family (i). What hh-control adds on top of the existing family (ii) is a spatially non-uniform confidence map: we replace the global scalar weight λσt\lambda_{\sigma_{t}} of Eq. (21) by the warp-derived mask MM over latent sites, so the surrogate is applied at full strength on observed sites and zero on −M1\!-\!M, recovering most of the Jacobian’s spatial-information content at zero autograd cost. The complementary inner block-conditional Gibbs refinement on −M1\!-\!M (Section 3) is what closes the gap on the unobserved support that family (ii) leaves open by construction.

Appendix C Block-conditional pseudo-Gibbs sampling

This appendix reads hh-control’s inner refinement loop as a block-conditional pseudo-Gibbs Markov chain: we recall the generalized DAE / pseudo-Gibbs framework of Bengio et al. [2013], prove Proposition 1 as its sub-state extension targeting the partial-observation conditional law, and contrast the resulting chain with SRVS [Jang et al., 2026]. All notation follows Section 2: the pretrained latent flow-matching model induces a velocity field uθ​(zk,tk,c)u_{\theta}(z_{k},t_{k},c) and a clean-prediction estimator z^0​(zk,tk,c)=zk−σk​uθ​(zk,tk,c)\hat{z}_{0}(z_{k},t_{k},c)=z_{k}-\sigma_{k}\,u_{\theta}(z_{k},t_{k},c) via Eq. (1).

C.1 Generalized denoising auto-encoders as generative models

Let XX denote the clean random variable and X~\tilde{X} its corruption under a fixed conditional 𝒞⁡(X~∣X)\mathcal{C}(\tilde{X}\mid X). Bengio et al. [2013] define the pseudo-Gibbs Markov chain associated with a learned reconstruction conditional Pθ​(X∣X~)P_{\theta}(X\mid\tilde{X}) as

X(j)∼Pθ​(X∣X~(j−1)),X~(j)∼𝒞⁡(X~∣X(j)),X^{(j)}\;\sim\;P_{\theta}(X\mid\tilde{X}^{(j-1)}),\qquad\tilde{X}^{(j)}\;\sim\;\mathcal{C}(\tilde{X}\mid X^{(j)}), (23)

with transition operator T⁡(X(j)∣X(j−1))=∫Pθ​(X(j)∣X~)​𝒞​(X~∣X(j−1))​𝑑X~T(X^{(j)}\mid X^{(j-1)})=\int P_{\theta}(X^{(j)}\mid\tilde{X})\,\mathcal{C}(\tilde{X}\mid X^{(j-1)})\,d\tilde{X} on XX. Their Theorem 1 states that if (i) PθP_{\theta} is a consistent estimator of the true posterior p⁡(X∣X~)p(X\mid\tilde{X}) induced by the joint p⁡(X)​𝒞​(X~∣X)p(X)\,\mathcal{C}(\tilde{X}\mid X), and (ii) TT is ergodic (positivity of PθP_{\theta} and 𝒞\mathcal{C} on a bounded volume is sufficient), then the asymptotic distribution of Eq. (23) converges to the data-generating distribution p⁡(X)p(X).

Translated to a latent flow-matching generator at fixed sampling step kk, the identifications 𝒞↔Rσk\mathcal{C}\!\leftrightarrow\!R_{\sigma_{k}} (re-noising at level σk\sigma_{k}) and Pθ↔DσkP_{\theta}\!\leftrightarrow\!D_{\sigma_{k}} (the implicit conditional induced by the denoiser/clean-prediction estimator z^0​(⋅,tk,c)\hat{z}_{0}(\cdot,t_{k},c)) give a perturb-and-redenoise iteration on zkz_{k} at fixed σk\sigma_{k}. Section C.2 extends this primitive to the partial-observation conditional setting that hh-control’s inner loop targets.

C.2 Sub-state ergodicity and stationary distribution

This subsection proves Proposition 1 from Section 3.1 by reduction to a sub-state instance of Bengio et al. [2013] Theorem 1. Throughout we hold σt>0\sigma_{t}>0, mask MM, warped latent z~0\tilde{z}_{0}, and pin z¯t=(1−σt)​z~0+σt​ξobs\bar{z}_{t}=(1-\sigma_{t})\tilde{z}_{0}+\sigma_{t}\,\xi_{\rm obs} fixed; we write z|Mz|_{M} and z|1−Mz|_{1-M} for the corresponding restrictions of any latent tensor.

Lemma 1 (Sub-state DAE chain).

With z¯t|M\bar{z}_{t}|_{M} held as fixed exogenous context and σt\sigma_{t} held fixed, the inner-loop chain Eqs. (8)–(9) restricted to coordinates in −M1\!-\!M is a generalized DAE chain in the sense of Bengio et al. [2013], with substitutions X↔z0|1−MX\!\leftrightarrow\!z_{0}|_{1-M} and X~↔z~|1−M\tilde{X}\!\leftrightarrow\!\tilde{z}|_{1-M}.

Proof of Lemma 1.

The corruption restricted to −M1\!-\!M is 𝒞⁡(z~|1−M​∣z0|1−M)=𝒩⁡((1−σt)​z0|1−M,σt2​I)\mathcal{C}(\tilde{z}|_{1-M}\mid z_{0}|_{1-M})=\mathcal{N}\!\bigl((1-\sigma_{t})\,z_{0}|_{1-M},\,\sigma_{t}^{2}\,I\bigr), a full-support Gaussian on z0|1−Mz_{0}|_{1-M}. The conditional reconstruction Pθ​(z0|1−M​∣z~|1−M,z~|M=z¯t|M)P_{\theta}(z_{0}|_{1-M}\mid\tilde{z}|_{1-M},\,\tilde{z}|_{M}{=}\bar{z}_{t}|_{M}) is the implicit conditional induced by the denoiser uθ​(⋅,t,c)u_{\theta}(\cdot,t,c) applied to the perturbed iterate with the observed coordinates pinned at z¯t|M\bar{z}_{t}|_{M}. Coordinates in MM are never re-noised during the inner loop; they remain pinned to z¯t|M\bar{z}_{t}|_{M}, so the chain on −M1\!-\!M is a generalized DAE chain with z¯t|M\bar{z}_{t}|_{M} as fixed exogenous context. ∎

Proof of Proposition 1.

By Lemma 1, the chain on −M1\!-\!M is a generalized DAE chain with z¯t|M\bar{z}_{t}|_{M} as fixed exogenous context. Bengio et al. [2013] Theorem 1 states that if the reconstruction conditional PθP_{\theta} is consistent with the true posterior p⁡(X∣X~)p(X\mid\tilde{X}) induced by the joint p⁡(X)​𝒞​(X~∣X)p(X)\,\mathcal{C}(\tilde{X}\mid X), and the transition operator is ergodic on a bounded volume, then the chain’s asymptotic distribution converges to the data-generating distribution p⁡(X)p(X). In our setting, the joint at level σt\sigma_{t} is conditioned on z¯t|M\bar{z}_{t}|_{M}, so p⁡(X)↔p⁡(z0|1−M​∣z¯t|M)p(X)\!\leftrightarrow\!p(z_{0}|_{1-M}\mid\bar{z}_{t}|_{M}). Under assumption (A1), Pθ↔uθP_{\theta}\!\leftrightarrow\!u_{\theta} is consistent with this conditional joint; under (A2), positivity of the perturbation kernel on −M1\!-\!M gives ergodicity. Therefore the clean-prediction iterates converge in distribution to p⁡(z0|1−M​∣z¯t|M)p(z_{0}|_{1-M}\mid\bar{z}_{t}|_{M}). ∎

Connection to coordinate descent / block Gibbs sampling.

The chain restricts the perturb-and-redenoise primitive to a fixed coordinate block −M1\!-\!M while holding MM frozen. This is the generative-modeling analog of block-coordinate descent in optimization, in which a fixed subset of variables is updated at each iteration with the rest held constant; here “descent” on a loss is replaced by “mixing” of an implicit prior. The use of a fixed block (rather than random or systematic scans across blocks) is a deliberate task-driven choice: the partition (−M,M)(1\!-\!M,M) is given by the camera-control mask geometry and is the same at every probe jj.

C.3 Comparison with SRVS

The pseudo-Gibbs chain primitive is shared with Self-Refining Video Sampling (SRVS, Jang et al. [2026]). At a fixed denoising step with noise level σk\sigma_{k}, SRVS iterates

zk(j)=(1−σk)​z^0(j−1)+σk​ξ(j),z^0(j)=zk(j)−σk​uθ​(zk(j),tk,c),ξ(j)∼𝒩⁡(0,I).z_{k}^{(j)}\;=\;(1-\sigma_{k})\,\hat{z}_{0}^{(j-1)}\;+\;\sigma_{k}\,\xi^{(j)},\qquad\hat{z}_{0}^{(j)}\;=\;z_{k}^{(j)}\;-\;\sigma_{k}\,u_{\theta}(z_{k}^{(j)},t_{k},c),\qquad\xi^{(j)}\!\sim\!\mathcal{N}(0,I). (24)

With identifications X↔z^0X\!\leftrightarrow\!\hat{z}_{0}, X~↔zk\tilde{X}\!\leftrightarrow\!z_{k}, 𝒞↔Rσk\mathcal{C}\!\leftrightarrow\!R_{\sigma_{k}} and Pθ↔DσkP_{\theta}\!\leftrightarrow\!D_{\sigma_{k}}, Eq. (24) is a structural instance of Eq. (23): SRVS uses Bengio’s pseudo-Gibbs primitive at the chain level. The original SRVS paper invokes this informally — it does not state or apply Theorem 1 of Bengio et al. [2013] explicitly — and motivates the practice as “mode-seeking” toward the data manifold. Beyond the chain primitive, SRVS adds an outer selective-refinement scheme applied between outer steps as a per-iteration mixing rule on the next-level noisy latent zti+1(k)z_{t_{i+1}}^{(k)}, with the eligibility mask derived from the lag-1 self-disagreement statistic U⁡(z(k−1),z(k))=1C​‖Dθ​(z(k−1))−Dθ​(z(k))‖1U(z^{(k-1)},z^{(k)})\!=\!\frac{1}{C}\|D_{\theta}(z^{(k-1)})-D_{\theta}(z^{(k)})\|_{1} thresholded at a fixed τ\tau. Both the inner chain and the outer mixing rule act on every coordinate of the latent; SRVS does not condition the chain on any external observation.

Where hh-control differs.

hh-control extends Bengio’s primitive in five non-degenerate respects.

(i) Conditional vs. unconditional target (theorem correctness). The inner chain runs on the unobserved sub-state z|1−Mz|_{1-M} with the observed coordinates pinned at the freshly noised observation z¯t|M=(1−σt)​z~0|M+σt​ξobs|M\bar{z}_{t}|_{M}=(1-\sigma_{t})\tilde{z}_{0}|_{M}+\sigma_{t}\,\xi_{\rm obs}|_{M}. Proposition 1 extends Bengio’s Theorem 1 to the sub-state setting and proves that the chain’s stationary distribution is the partial-observation conditional data law p⁡(z0|1−M​∣z¯t|M)p(z_{0}|_{1-M}\!\mid\!\bar{z}_{t}|_{M}). SRVS targets the unconditional p⁡(z0)p(z_{0}) informally without a formal theorem statement or proof; hh-control’s claim is sharper, conditioned on the observed evidence, and proven.

(ii) Block-conditional vs. full-state chain (the algorithmic novelty). hh-control acts on the fixed coordinate block −M1\!-\!M given by the warp-derived mask, and within −M1\!-\!M updates 3D patches of latent voxels jointly. The patch partition is justified by the order-2-Markov locality validation of Section D and is what makes the sub-state chain feasible at video scale: the full-state chain on the ∼105\sim\!10^{5} Wan 2.2 latent sites would mix slowly per inner-iteration budget. SRVS does not partition the state; the chain is full-state and the only spatial structure is per-coordinate.

(iii) Mask source and mask placement. SRVS’s eligibility mask is implicit (model self-disagreement) and applied outside the inner chain, as a mixing rule between outer steps. hh-control’s mask is external (camera-warp visibility) and defines the partition (M,1−M)(M,1-M) that the inner chain itself respects: observed sites are pinned, unobserved sites are refined. The role the mask plays in the algorithm is categorically different in the two methods.

(iv) Convergence diagnostic. SRVS gates refinement by the lag-1 paired-probe self-disagreement U⁡(z(k−1),z(k))<τU(z^{(k-1)},z^{(k)})<\tau, which requires a noise-aware τ⁡(σk)\tau(\sigma_{k}) to remain calibrated across the schedule. hh-control uses the per-patch Δ\Delta-Welford running-variance plateau detector Eq. (12) with a single relative threshold κ∈(0,1]\kappa\!\in\!(0,1] that is scale-free at the patch level and works unchanged across all outer steps; the per-patch granularity matches the locality scale at which neighboring coordinates’ chain trajectories are correlated.

(v) Readout from the inner loop. SRVS commits the last iterate z^0(Kf)\hat{z}_{0}^{(K_{f})} as the inner-loop output. hh-control consumes the Polyak-averaged readout z¯0=Jmax−1​∑jz^0(j)\bar{z}_{0}\!=\!J_{\max}^{-1}\sum_{j}\hat{z}_{0}^{(j)}, which feeds the FlowMatch Euler step a τint/Jmax\sqrt{\tau_{\rm int}/J_{\max}}-times more concentrated estimator of the stationary mean at one in-place accumulator’s cost (Section E).

In short, the genuinely new theoretical contribution of hh-control is (i): the sub-state extension of Bengio’s Theorem 1 with a pinned exogenous context, giving the inner chain a proven stationary distribution equal to the partial-observation conditional posterior. The genuinely new algorithmic contribution is (ii): the block-conditional Gibbs primitive on patches of the unobserved support, made adaptive by the per-patch Δ\Delta-Welford gate and locality-justified at video scale. Neither contribution exists in SRVS or in any prior generalized-DAE-based sampler we are aware of.

Appendix D Block-precision locality validation

Setup.

Stack the NN VAE-encoded videos into a tensor of shape (N,C,L,H,W)(N,C,L,H,W), with CC-channel voxel zl,h,w(n)∈ℝCz^{(n)}_{l,h,w}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{C} at grid position (l,h,w)(l,h,w) of video nn. Following Section 3.2, we work one axis at a time. For axis α∈{L,H,W}\alpha\!\in\!\{L,H,W\}, an axis-aligned line stack is built by permuting α\alpha to slot 11 and the channel dim to slot 22, then merging the two off-axis dimensions and the video index into one row index:

(N,C,L,H,W)→permute + flatten off-axis(Ns,|α|,C),Ns=N⋅∏α′≠α|α′|.(N,C,L,H,W)\;\;\xrightarrow{\;\text{permute + flatten off-axis}\;}\;\;\bigl(N_{s},\,|\alpha|,\,C\bigr),\qquad N_{s}\,=\,N\!\cdot\!\prod_{\alpha^{\prime}\neq\alpha}|\alpha^{\prime}|.

Each row of this (Ns,|α|,C)\bigl(N_{s},|\alpha|,C\bigr) tensor is one line 𝐗=(X1,…,X|α|)∈ℝ|α|×C\mathbf{X}\!=\!(X_{1},\dots,X_{|\alpha|})\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{|\alpha|\times C}: the |α||\alpha| voxels swept along α\alpha at one (video, off-axis location) pair, with Xβ∈ℝCX_{\beta}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{C} the voxel at axis-position β\beta. Treating the NsN_{s} rows as i.i.d. draws of the joint 𝐗\mathbf{X} — under a working assumption of stationarity along the off-axis dimensions — and flattening the last two dimensions gives the design matrix 𝐅∈ℝNs×|α|​C\mathbf{F}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{N_{s}\times|\alpha|C} that the precision pipeline below consumes. For the benchmarked Wan 2.2 latent at 4949 frames, 704×1280704{\times}1280, C=48C\!=\!48, this yields Ns∈[×104,×105]N_{s}\!\in\![2.9\!\times\!10^{4},\,1.8\!\times\!10^{5}] depending on axis, comfortably Ns≫|α|​CN_{s}\gg|\alpha|C.

Block precision and conditional independence.

Form the centered sample covariance

Σ^=1Ns−1​𝐅⊤​𝐅∈ℝ|α|​C×|α|​C,\widehat{\Sigma}\;=\;\tfrac{1}{N_{s}-1}\,\mathbf{F}^{\top}\mathbf{F}\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{|\alpha|C\times|\alpha|C},

where 𝐅∈ℝNs×|α|​C\mathbf{F}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{s}\times|\alpha|C} stacks the NsN_{s} flattened lines after per-coordinate standardization. Add a tiny relative ridge Σ^λ=Σ^+λ​tr​(Σ^)/(|α|​C)​I\widehat{\Sigma}_{\lambda}=\widehat{\Sigma}+\lambda\,\mathrm{tr}(\widehat{\Sigma})/(|\alpha|C)\,I (λ=10−6\lambda=10^{-6}) for positive-definiteness and form the precision Ω^=Σ^λ−1\widehat{\Omega}=\widehat{\Sigma}_{\lambda}^{-1} via numerically stable Cholesky factorization. Reshape Ω^\widehat{\Omega} into a |α|×|α||\alpha|\!\times\!|\alpha| array of (C×C)(C\!\times\!C) blocks {Ω^β​γ}\{\widehat{\Omega}_{\beta\gamma}\} indexed by axis positions β,γ∈{1,…,|α|}\beta,\gamma\!\in\!\{1,\dots,|\alpha|\}. The classical Gauss–Markov result [Rogers and Williams, 2000] extended block-wise reads

Xβ⟂⟂Xγ|X−β​γ⟺Ω^β​γ=0C×C,X_{\beta}\;\perp\!\!\!\perp\;X_{\gamma}\,\bigm|\,X_{-\beta\gamma}\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\widehat{\Omega}_{\beta\gamma}=0_{C\times C}, (25)

where X−β​γ={Xr:r≠β,γ}X_{-\beta\gamma}=\{X_{r}:r\neq\beta,\gamma\} is the rest of the line.

Block partial correlation via canonical correlations.

The natural unit-free statistic is the block partial correlation

R^β​γ=−Ω^β​β−1/2Ω^β​γΩ^γ​γ−1/2∈ℝC×C,\widehat{R}_{\beta\gamma}\;=\;-\,\widehat{\Omega}_{\beta\beta}^{-1/2}\,\widehat{\Omega}_{\beta\gamma}\,\widehat{\Omega}_{\gamma\gamma}^{-1/2}\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{C\times C},

whose singular values ρ1≥⋯≥ρC≥0\rho_{1}\geq\dots\geq\rho_{C}\geq 0 are the canonical partial correlations between XβX_{\beta} and XγX_{\gamma} after regressing out X−β​γX_{-\beta\gamma}. The top canonical correlation ρ1​(R^β​γ)∈[0,1]\rho_{1}(\widehat{R}_{\beta\gamma})\in[0,1] measures the strongest linear conditional dependence; vanishing of all ρi\rho_{i} recovers the conditional-independence test of Eq. (25). On the diagonal β=γ\beta\!=\!\gamma, R^β​β=−I\widehat{R}_{\beta\beta}=-I and all singular values equal 11 (the source of the |α|×|α||\alpha|\!\times\!|\alpha| heatmap diagonal in Figure 2).

Decay metric.

For each axis we report the cumulative tail mass of the squared top canonical partial correlation,

η⁡(r)=∑|β−γ|>r(ρ1​(R^β​γ))2∑β≠γ(ρ1​(R^β​γ))2∈[0,1].\eta(r)\;=\;\frac{\sum_{|\beta-\gamma|>r}\bigl(\rho_{1}(\widehat{R}_{\beta\gamma})\bigr)^{2}}{\sum_{\beta\neq\gamma}\bigl(\rho_{1}(\widehat{R}_{\beta\gamma})\bigr)^{2}}\;\in\;[0,1]. (26)

η⁡(r)\eta(r) is the fraction of squared off-diagonal partial-correlation mass at distance greater than rr; sharp locality ⇔\Leftrightarrow η⁡(r)→0\eta(r)\to 0 for some modest rr.

Noise floor.

A finite-sample top canonical correlation between two unrelated CC-vectors averages to 𝔼⁡[ρ1]≈2​C/Ns\mathbb{E}[\rho_{1}]\!\approx\!2\sqrt{C/N_{s}} rather than zero. For our axes this gives floors of 0.0330.033 (LL), 0.0610.061 (HH), 0.0820.082 (WW); observed far-distance values are 0.070.07–0.100.10, within a factor of ∼2\sim\!2 of the theoretical prediction. Most residual mass at large distances is sampling noise rather than true long-range coupling.

Reading Figure 2.

Each axis gives a |α|×|α||\alpha|\!\times\!|\alpha| heatmap of ρ1​(R^β​γ)\rho_{1}(\widehat{R}_{\beta\gamma}). A clean local axis satisfies (i) ρ1≥0.5\rho_{1}\geq 0.5 at |β−γ|=1|\beta-\gamma|=1, (ii) drop to ≤1/3\leq\!1/3 of that value by |β−γ|=2|\beta-\gamma|=2, (iii) floor near 2​C/Ns2\sqrt{C/N_{s}} for |β−γ|≥3|\beta-\gamma|\geq 3. Figure 2 satisfies all three on each of L,H,WL,H,W for the Wan 2.2 latent, justifying the choice of patch radius ≥2\geq 2 voxels in Section 3.2.

Locality across the noise schedule.

The diagnostic above applies to clean VAE-encoded latents. We extend it to the model’s clean prediction z^0​(zt,t,c)\hat{z}_{0}(z_{t},t,c) at non-zero noise levels, since the inner-loop perturb-and-redenoise of Eqs. (8)–(9) operates in clean-prediction space at the current noise level σt\sigma_{t}. We generate 200200 videos by running the official Wan 2.2 flow-matching sampler from random initial noise z1∼𝒩⁡(0,I)z_{1}\!\sim\!\mathcal{N}(0,I) down to z0z_{0}, and record the full sampling trajectory {zt}\{z_{t}\}. At every recorded denoising step we evaluate z^0​(zt,t,c)=zt−σt​uθ​(zt,t,c)\hat{z}_{0}(z_{t},t,c)=z_{t}-\sigma_{t}u_{\theta}(z_{t},t,c) and run the block-precision pipeline of Eq. (25) on the resulting z^0\hat{z}_{0} tensors at σt∈{0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9}\sigma_{t}\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9\}. Figure 6 shows the resulting per-axis heatmaps at all five noise levels: the diagonal band stays sharp at every σt\sigma_{t}, with off-diagonal mass dropping into the finite-sample noise floor by distance |β−γ|=2|\beta-\gamma|\!=\!2–33 on each of L,H,WL,H,W, identical to the clean-latent diagnostic of Figure 2. The locality structure is therefore preserved across the entire sampling trajectory, not just on clean encoded latents, and the block-conditional Gibbs partition of Section 3.2 is valid at every active hh-control outer step.

Appendix E Polyak-averaged readout: compatibility with the FlowMatch Euler step

The write-back Eq. (10) consumes the running mean z¯0=Jmax−1​∑j=1Jmaxz^0(j)\bar{z}_{0}=J_{\max}^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{J_{\max}}\hat{z}_{0}^{(j)} of the inner clean-prediction iterates, not the last iterate. The variance reduction argument is the standard MCMC iterate-averaging result [Polyak and Juditsky, 1992]: at stationarity the running mean has variance σπ2​τint/J+𝒪⁡(J−2)\sigma_{\pi}^{2}\,\tau_{\rm int}/J+\mathcal{O}(J^{-2}) vs. the last iterate’s σπ2\sigma_{\pi}^{2}, where τint\tau_{\rm int} is the integrated autocorrelation time. We add only the observation that this estimator is the right input to feed into our outer integrator. The FlowMatch Euler update zk+1=zk+(σk+1−σk)​(zk−z^0final)/σkz_{k+1}=z_{k}+(\sigma_{k+1}-\sigma_{k})\,(z_{k}-\hat{z}_{0}^{\rm final})/\sigma_{k} is linear in z^0final\hat{z}_{0}^{\rm final}, so any extra variance in the readout is injected into the latent zk+1z_{k+1} without an averaging or projection step to absorb it; conversely, the bias/variance decomposition of the Polyak-averaged readout passes through the linear update unchanged. Consuming the running mean therefore hands the integrator a τint/Jmax\sqrt{\tau_{\rm int}/J_{\max}}-times more concentrated estimator of the stationary mean than the last iterate would, at the cost of one in-place accumulator per outer step — a strict improvement under the linearity that FlowMatch already provides.

Appendix F Toy-example details

We have provided the code of the toy example for reproducing all the figures in the paper.

Setup. The unconditional density is a 2D 8-square checkerboard: eight unit squares centered at {(i+0.5,j+0.5):i,j∈{−2,−1,0,1},(i+j)mod 2=0}\{(i+0.5,j+0.5):i,j\in\{-2,-1,0,1\},(i+j)\,\mathrm{mod}\,2=0\}, sampled uniform-area within each square. We train a 6-layer flow-matching MLP with sinusoidal time embedding and SiLU\mathrm{SiLU} activations on this density for 20,00020{,}000 iterations (batch 512512, AdamW with lr=2×10−3\mathrm{lr}=2{\times}10^{-3} and weight decay 10−410^{-4}, cosine schedule); the trained MLP attains a manifold-hit rate above 99%99\% on unconditional samples, certifying that any conditional shortfall observed below is due to the conditional sampler rather than a poorly trained prior. We then evaluate conditional sampling under a noisy partial observation of the first coordinate y∼𝒩⁡(z0​[1],σy2)y\!\sim\!\mathcal{N}(z_{0}[1],\,\sigma_{y}^{2}) with σy=0.2\sigma_{y}\!=\!0.2, anchored at yobs≈0.5y_{\rm obs}\!\approx\!0.5 where the vertical constraint line intersects exactly two of the eight filled squares, yielding a binary mode-coverage question with two well-separated conditional modes.

Evaluation. We compare hh-control against DPS [Chung et al., 2022] (compute-native at NFE=100\mathrm{NFE}\!=\!100, 11 forward ++ 11 backward per step at 5050 outer steps) and TFG-UGD [Ye et al., 2024] at NFE=250\mathrm{NFE}\!=\!250 (configuration Nrecur=2N_{\rm recur}\!=\!2, Niter=1N_{\rm iter}\!=\!1, μ=0.5\mu\!=\!0.5, ρ=0.5\rho\!=\!0.5, giving 55 calls per step at 5050 outer steps). hh-control with inner budget J=4J\!=\!4 also costs 55 calls per step (11 outer forward ++ 44 inner forwards), so it is compute-matched to TFG-UGD at NFE=250\mathrm{NFE}\!=\!250. For the matched sweep of Figure 1, we vary J∈{0,…,16}J\!\in\!\{0,\dots,16\} for hh-control and Nrecur∈{1,…,6}N_{\rm recur}\!\in\!\{1,\dots,6\} for TFG-UGD, plotting total NFE on the horizontal axis.

Each method is evaluated with 1010 seeds and 500500 samples per seed (5,0005{,}000 samples total). The posterior-hit rate is the fraction of samples falling both inside one of the two filled squares intersected by the constraint line and within |x1−yobs|<0.5|x_{1}-y_{\rm obs}|<0.5 of the anchor. A sample on the constraint line but outside the filled squares contributes zero to posterior-hit but may still contribute to manifold-hit (a sanity check that the sampler did not drift entirely off the data manifold).

Results. Figure 1 bins the inner iterations jj by noise band and plots |ΔW(j)||\Delta_{W}^{(j)}| (averaged over the population of toy chains) on a shared horizontal axis with the posterior-hit rate of Figure 1; the two curves plateau over the same jj-range, the empirical content of the claim that |ΔW(j)|→0|\Delta_{W}^{(j)}|\!\to\!0 is a reliable ground-truth-free trigger for the early-freeze gate. Disabling the inner loop (J=0J\!=\!0) reduces hh-control to DPS-like behaviour: with the inner Gibbs chain in Eqs. (8)–(9) disabled, only the outer soft pull of Eq. (5) remains, which at the σy=0.2\sigma_{y}\!=\!0.2 used here is the DPS gradient evaluated at the flow-matching Tweedie mean (Appendix B.4). The hh-control sample cloud then collapses onto the same constraint-line support that DPS produces in Figure 1, with mode coverage governed entirely by the outer pull — the clean ablation that isolates the inner loop as the source of the mode-coverage gain.

Appendix G hh-control implementation details

G.1 Hyperparameter Settings

Table 4 lists the necessary hyperparameters used in our main experiments with hh-control on the Wan 2.2 backbone. The discretized FlowMatch sampler runs for 5050 outer steps, indexed so that step 00 corresponds to pure noise and step 5050 to the clean sample. The camera-control window covers outer steps ts=2t_{s}\!=\!2 through te=5t_{e}\!=\!5, the highest-noise interval where the warp constraint is most informative; at each step within this window the inner-loop refinement runs with budget Jmax=10J_{\max}\!=\!10, with the Δ\Delta-Welford freeze gate (Section 3.2) allowing per-patch early termination so that the realised inner iteration count averages below JmaxJ_{\max}. We use classifier-free guidance with scale 4.04.0.

Appendix H Datasets and evaluation protocol

RealEstate10K. We follow the RealEstate10K [Zhou et al., 2018] train/test split. Sampling. We sample 200200 scenes uniformly at random, with a fixed seed for reproducibility. For each scene we treat the first frame as the I2V conditioning input and the remaining 4848 frames as the held-out reference under the source camera trajectory. Reference-based metrics (LPIPS, SSIM) are computed between the generated video and the held-out reference frames after matching frame counts. The target trajectory is the one parsed from the dataset’s pose annotations; it is fed to every method that takes camera parameters explicitly, and used to render the warp for every training-free method that takes a warp.

DAVIS controlled-trajectory synthesis We take the DAVIS-2017 challenge set, restricted to the 2828 sequences with continuous moderate-to-large object motion. For each scene we synthesize three target trajectories of varying angular extent — approximately ±15∘\pm 15^{\circ}, ±30∘\pm 30^{\circ}, and ±45∘\pm 45^{\circ} horizontal sweep around the source camera — giving 8484 controlled-trajectory videos in total. Each trajectory is realized as a smooth 4949-frame sequence of 66-DOF camera poses; they are converted into a warp by the same depth-based lift-and-reproject pipeline used by every training-free baseline (see Appendix G). DAVIS lacks ground-truth novel views under the synthesized trajectories, so we do not report PSNR/LPIPS/SSIM and instead use FVD against the source distribution and the camera-pose-derived trajectory metrics on re-extracted poses (Section H.1).

H.1 Camera trajectory metrics

For every generated video we re-extract the 4949-frame camera trajectory with Mega-SAM [Li et al., 2025], a recent monocular SLAM tracker, without any tuning. The re-extracted trajectory is aligned to the target trajectory by a single similarity transform (translation, rotation, scale) and then evaluated by:

  • •

    ATE (Absolute Trajectory Error): per-frame root-mean-square translational error after alignment, in centimeters under the dataset’s metric scale.

  • •

    RRE (Relative Rotation Error): per-pair root-mean-square rotational error between consecutive frames, in degrees.

  • •

    RTE (Relative Translation Error): per-pair root-mean-square translational error between consecutive frames, in centimeters.

Failures of Mega-SAM (re-extraction divergence on extreme dynamic content) are extremely rare on RealEstate10K and occur on <3%<\!3\% of DAVIS trajectories; affected videos are dropped uniformly across all methods to keep the comparison fair, with the drop count reported per row.

H.2 Perceptual metrics

FVD. Standard Fréchet Video Distance [Unterthiner et al., 2018] computed against a held-out reference distribution per dataset: source DAVIS clips on DAVIS, source RealEstate10K clips on RealEstate10K. Features come from the I3D backbone trained on Kinetics-400; we use the public implementation with default centering.

CLIP-v / CLIP-f. CLIP-based video coherence (CLIP-v, mean cosine similarity of frame-CLIP embeddings within the same video) and frame-text alignment (CLIP-f, mean cosine similarity between each frame’s CLIP image embedding and the scene caption’s CLIP text embedding). These are the two text-aligned consistency metrics commonly used.

LPIPS. Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity [Zhang et al., 2018]: a reference-based perceptual metric that compares deep features (we use the standard AlexNet backbone) between two RGB frames, calibrated to human perceptual judgments. We report LPIPS only on RealEstate10K, where each generated frame can be compared to a held-out ground-truth view at the corresponding pose; DAVIS provides no such reference for novel-trajectory views. Lower is better.

SSIM. Structural Similarity Index [Wang et al., 2004]: a classical reference-based metric that compares the luminance, contrast, and structural components of two RGB frames in a sliding window. As with LPIPS, we report SSIM only on RealEstate10K against the held-out ground-truth view, computed per frame and averaged over the video. Higher is better.

H.3 Inference speed

Table 5 reports inference speed in frames/min on a single NVIDIA A40 GPU at each method’s native operating resolution. hh-control runs at 7.137.13 frames/min at the full 720×1280720{\times}1280 resolution shared by every training-free baseline—the second-fastest method overall, behind only TTM (12.9912.99), which is bare hard-replacement without any inner-loop refinement and therefore represents the natural runtime ceiling. The inner-loop pseudo-Gibbs refinement adds modest overhead relative to TTM, yet hh-control remains faster than the remaining training-free baselines (WorldForge 3.923.92, RePaint 6.236.23, Coarse-Guided 6.976.97) and faster than every training-based controller, even though the training-based methods operate at strictly lower resolution (ReCamMaster 5.555.55 at 480×832480{\times}832, TrajectoryCrafter 4.424.42 at 384×672384{\times}672, TrajectoryAttention 1.361.36 at 576×1024576{\times}1024). Combined with the FVD gains of Tables 1–2, this places hh-control on the favourable side of the quality–speed Pareto frontier.

Appendix I Additional qualitative results

I.1 Failure-mode catalogue

Figure 7 compares the warped guidance video (with depth-induced wrong warping), the ground-truth target trajectory, and our hh-control output. Although the inner-loop refinement still produces visually plausible inpainting on the unobserved complement (the generated frames are seam-free and natural-looking), the output tracks the wrongly warped guidance rather than the ground-truth trajectory. This is the expected behaviour under our partial-observation framing (Section 3): the warped video supplies the posterior evidence, and once that evidence is geometrically inconsistent the pretrained prior cannot correct it, since the prior encodes what plausible video looks like rather than what the correct camera trajectory should be. Robustness to severe depth misestimation therefore requires either a more reliable depth estimator upstream or a separate trajectory prior beyond the visual prior p⁡(z0)p(z_{0}).

I.2 RealEstate10K

Figure 8 extends the main-paper qualitative panel (Figure 3) with additional held-out RealEstate10K scenes spanning a broader range of trajectory extents.

I.3 DAVIS

Figure 9 extends the main-paper DAVIS qualitative panel (Figure 4) with additional dynamic scenes under larger trajectory sweeps.

Appendix J Broader impacts

Positive impacts.

Improved camera control for pretrained video generators has constructive applications in filmmaking previsualization, simulation and synthetic data for embodied AI, virtual- and augmented-reality content authoring, and education. Because hh-control is training-free and adds no new generative capability on top of the base model, it lowers the engineering barrier to high-quality camera-controlled video without requiring new large-scale training, which improves accessibility for users without the compute to fine-tune video generators.

Negative impacts.

Higher-fidelity camera control on pretrained video generators can also make synthetic video more convincing, which inherits the well-known misuse profile of modern video generative models—non-consensual or deceptive synthetic media, impersonation, and disinformation. hh-control itself does not introduce new training data or new generative capacity; it operates as a sampler on top of an already-released backbone, so the risks it raises are the risks of the underlying generator combined with sharper trajectory control.

Mitigations.

We rely on the safeguards of the underlying pretrained video generator (content filters, license restrictions, watermarking where applicable), release no new pretrained model or scraped dataset, and use only public benchmarks (RealEstate10K, DAVIS) under their original terms.
